source: A moving rod makes an emf, the current feels a force, and someone has to keep pulling.
Students get the current's direction backward: the induced current always opposes the motion.

A rod sliding on rails is the simplest generator. It joins Motional emf, Ohm's law and the force on a current, with Lenz's law deciding every direction. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

$$\role[emf]{voltage}{\varepsilon} = \role[magnetic field]{field}{B}\role[rod length]{position}{L}\role{velocity}{v}, \qquad \role{current}{I} = \frac{\role[emf]{voltage}{\varepsilon}}{\role{resistance}{R}}, \qquad F = ILB = \frac{B^2L^2v}{R}.$$ The magnetic force always opposes the motion, so something must keep pulling; its power $Fv$ equals the heating $I^2R$. With a steady pull $F$, the rod settles at $v_t = FR/(B^2L^2)$.
As the rod moves right the loop's area grows. The red dots show the induced current, and the red arrow the force that opposes the motion.
A rod $0.40\ \text{m}$ long slides at $3.0\ \text{m/s}$ on rails joined by $2.0\ \Omega$, in a $0.50\ \text{T}$ field. Find (1) the emf, (2) the current and (3) the pulling force needed.
Getting the current's direction backward. The induced current must push back on the rod; if your current would speed the rod up, energy would come from nowhere. Check with $F = IL \times B$.
